subject: Branch Returning Two Values When it is Expecting 1

messages.author: 6cc0fd77b5c1b0a7
messages.subject: Branch Returning Two Values When it is Expecting 1
parts:
Hi,

Thanks in advance for the help.  I'm trying to get a grasp on all of the features here
 
I figured to teach myself I would try to recreate the dice game they explain in the book The Goal which demonstrates process bottlenecks (https://maaw.info/MatchBowlExperiment.htm) .  The basic principle of the game is that a player rolls a dice and they pass the rolled number of whatever object people are using into an inventory buffer to show the work done that day.  The next player rolls the die and they move that number of objects, if they are available in the upstream inventory buffer;  if there enough objects available as the dice roll, the downstream player can only move the number of objects in the upstream buffer.  This trend can continue for however many turns and players as one wants.

The following code was basically what I came up with.  The first dice roll sets an attribute which is used to control the number of objects passed to Player 1.  At this point I cannot figure out how to control the release of the objects, so Player 2 will only seize the available inventory of Player 1 if the second die roll exceeds the available inventory of Player 1.  I thought I could use a branch to control the two tasks, but I am creating something that is accidentally evaluating 2 values and I get the following error:

Error: 'Turn1' at 2.00 in 'Branch':
 Expecting a single value: [extent=2].

Anyway, Here is the R code. Thanks so much for the help.  There is probably a much easier method for recreating this simulation.
------------------------------------------------------------------

library(tidyverse)
library(simmer)
library(simmer.plot)
library(simmer.bricks)

die.size <- 6

coin.sim <- simmer()

coin <- trajectory() %>%
  set_attribute("Roll 1", function(){sample(1:die.size, 1)}) %>%
  seize("Player 1", amount = function() {get_attribute(coin.sim, "Roll 1")}) %>%
  set_attribute("Roll 2", function(){sample(1:die.size, 1)}) %>%
  branch(option = function() {
    
    p1.sys <- coin.sim %>%
      get_mon_resources() %>%
      filter(resource == "Player 1",
             time == now(coin.sim)) %>%
      .$system
    
    ifelse(p1.sys > get_attribute(coin.sim, "Roll 2"), 1, 2)
  },
  continue = c(T, T),
  
  trajectory("enough") %>%
    timeout(1) %>%
    release("Player 1", amount = function() {get_attribute(coin.sim, "Roll 2")}),
  
  trajectory("not enough") %>%
    timeout(1) %>%
    release("Player 1", amount = function(){
      
      p1.sys <- coin.sim %>%
        get_mon_resources() %>%
        filter(resource == "Player 1",
               time == now(coin.sim)) %>%
        .$system
      })) %>%
  timeout(1) 

coin.sim <- simmer() %>%
  add_resource("Player 1", capacity = Inf) %>%
  add_resource("Player 2", capacity = Inf) %>%
  add_generator("Turn", coin, at(1:10), mon = 2)

coin.sim %>%
  run(5)

At this point I cannot figure out how to control the release of the objects, so Player 2 will only seize the available inventory of Player 1 if the second die roll exceeds the available inventory of Player 1. > Error: 'Turn1' at 2.00 in 'Branch':
> Expecting a single value: [extent=2].

As you observed, the 'option' function returned 2 values at some
point, while only one is expected. This is because you are using
ifelse, which is vectorised and thus the output length depends on the
condition length.

But there are other more important issues in your simulation. For
instance, 'get_mon_*' functions are not meant to be used during a
simulation, because they return the whole history, and this is very
inefficient. Yes, you can call them there, but that's definitely a bad
pattern.

At a higher abstraction level, you could simulate this problem in
several ways using simmer. But if you want to use resources, then you
cannot define a coin turn as an arrival process, because 1) coin turns
would leave seized resources behind (another bad pattern that will
raise a warning), and more importantly 2) they would try to release
resources from previous coin turns, which is not permitted in simmer
and raises an error. Instead, you need a single process and a looped
trajectory (see 'rollback').

But here there are no queues and no limits in the number of resources,
and therefore this problem involves no contention: you don't need
resources at all. You can implement this just using simple global
variables or attributes. But then, you don't need a DES!: the
definition of this problem is overly simplistic, and IMO using a DES
is completely overkilling.

In fact, you don't even need a loop. The simulation can be done very
efficiently in plain R as follows:

set.seed(42)
n_bowls <- 5
n_days <- 10
bowls <- rep(0, n_bowls)

out <- do.call(rbind, replicate(n_days, {
dice <- sample(6, n_bowls + 1, TRUE)
bowls <<- -diff(cummin(dice + c(0, -cumsum(bowls))))
list(dice, bowls)
}, simplify=FALSE))

dice <- do.call(rbind, out[,1])
bowls <- do.call(rbind, out[,2])

There you have a matrix of dice rolls for n_days and the status of the
bowls at the end of each day.

My advice: if you want to learn simmer, pick a more complex problem
(there are plenty of them in the vignettes); otherwise, you'll find
yourself trying to kill a fly with a gun.

Iñaki
